title: Chief Harry Wallace of the Unkechaug
summary: Chief Harry Wallace, also written Harry B. Wallace in some sources, is an Unkechaug leader, attorney, and advocate for sovereignty, language, community renewal, and Poospatuck Reservation life.
content:
Chief Harry Wallace, also identified as Harry B. Wallace in some sources, is a living contemporary Unkechaug leader, attorney, and advocate for sovereignty, language, community renewal, and life at the Poospatuck Reservation. The public sources cited here document leadership milestones beginning in 1991 and his election as chief in 1994, but they do not provide a verified birth date.

Historical Context

In 1991, Wallace opened a smoke shop on the reservation, part of a period of major political, economic, and cultural change in the community.1

On April 5, 1994, he was elected Chief of the Unkechaug, followed by community work around tribal unity, cultural revitalization, public grounds, and roads.12

Wallace also appears in community histories around economic development proposals, June Meeting, legal challenges, and sovereignty defense.13

Because Wallace is a living contemporary leader, this biography focuses on public leadership milestones and does not include private details.

Quoted Voice

In 1994, Wallace emphasized tribal unity and rights: I would like to emphasize that I am very positive about the composition and outlook of this council... We are strongly committed to preserving our sovereignty and to protecting our rights as an Indian nation and our traditions.1

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History, pp. 256, 260-261, 267-269.
  2. John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today, pp. 73-74.
  3. John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island, p. 169.
why_this_matters: Chief Wallace shows contemporary Indigenous sovereignty on Long Island. His biography connects governance, language revitalization, legal advocacy, community renewal, and continued Unkechaug life at Poospatuck.
